title: Multi-Agent Systems Wander Off Course Unless Something Watches the Goal
dek: Teams of LLM agents reach further than one model, and they drift further too. A field guide to the watcher, the workflow spec, the reuse rule and the paper trail.
by: Draft for team review · written by Claude Code from published research and engineering writing · checked in code
lead: What is a multi-agent system? Several LLM agents with their own roles and tools splitting one task. Its classic failure is goal drift, so give the team a cheap watcher, a written spec and exact-match reuse.

cover.alt: A team of agents drifting below a goal line, then pulled back by a steering agent with fast and slow paths.
cover.caption: A cheap check decides when to step in; the expensive reasoning runs only when drift shows.

description: What is a multi-agent system, and how do you keep one on task? A field guide to goal drift, workflow specs, safe result reuse and audit trails.
decisions: Which roles, inputs and tool permissions each agent gets, written as data
How often a watcher may step in, and how much each check may cost
What counts as an exact match before a stored result is reused
Which outputs must carry a reason or a source
When a task stays with a single agent

items.check: Write each agent's role, inputs, tools and goal into a spec the runtime reads.
items.why: Catches agents that quietly gain tools or lose sight of the goal.

items.check: Run a cheap drift check during long runs and log every intervention.
items.why: Catches a team that finishes confidently on the wrong question.

items.check: Use a separately prompted judge to score each run.
items.why: Catches an agent approving its own plan.

items.check: Limit each refinement round to one validated edit.
items.why: Catches broad rewrites that break components that already worked.

items.check: Key stored results on the full resolved request and execution context.
items.why: Catches a cached answer reused for a different question.

items.check: Require a reason with every decision and a source with every extracted value.
items.why: Catches answers nobody can audit or correct.

items.check: Remove one agent in a test run and watch what breaks.
items.why: Catches a team that collapses when a single member fails.

body.text: Put a watcher on the goal

body: Picture a team of agents that starts on a research question, calls tools for an hour, and ends up answering a different one. A new arXiv paper calls this goal drift: the system strays from its overall aim as the run goes on [3]. It wastes execution resources and produces outcomes nobody wanted [3]. Plan for this failure first.

So what is a multi-agent system? It is several LLM-driven agents, each with a role and tools, passing work between them to finish one task [3, 1]. That structure adds reach. In our view, it also adds places to drift. Every handoff restates the goal in another agent's words, and small slips add up over a long run.

The paper's answer is a steering agent that supervises the run live and pulls it back when drift shows [3]. It reads the execution context and splits its job in two. A cheap fast path decides when to step in, and a costly slow path decides how [3]. Both paths train together with RL, mixing a pairwise ranking objective with GRPO [3].

On information-seeking search tasks, the watcher improved both performance and efficiency for single agents and for teams [3]. It also handled out-of-domain tasks and unseen executors, and its intervention rate can be tuned without retraining [3]. We like the split most. A watcher that ran the expensive check on every step could cost more than the drift it prevents.

body.caption: How a steering agent supervises a running team without paying for deep reasoning on every step.
steps: Executor agents act and call tools
The steering agent reads the execution context
Fast path asks cheaply: is the run drifting?
If not, the run continues untouched
If so, the slow path writes an intervention
The team resumes, pointed back at the goal

body.text: Declare roles, inputs and tool permissions up front

body: Good workflows are hard to design ahead of time [1]. The authors of a subtitle translation system hit the same wall from the other side. Many agent systems, they note, run static workflows that ignore scene complexity and production context [4]. You still need a starting shape. The useful question is which parts of it must be explicit.

Inherit-MAS shows one explicit shape [1]. A meta-model writes a workflow of worker agents, each with a declared role, the messages it may receive and the tools it may use [1]. A judge, prompted separately, scores each executed candidate and diagnoses what went wrong [1]. That separation matters. An agent grading its own plan is a weak check.

Write the shape down as data instead of prose buried in a prompt. A spec you can diff is a spec you can review, and per-agent tool lists can be enforced by the runtime. We would add one field: the goal each agent serves, in one line. That gives a watcher like the steering agent something concrete to compare against [3].

body.label: Illustrative workflow spec: roles, inputs, tools and a separate judge
body.source:
workflow: cited-answer
goal: answer the user's question with cited evidence
agents:
  searcher:
    role: find candidate sources
    inputs: [goal, query_plan]
    tools: [web_search]
  reader:
    role: extract claims with their locations
    inputs: [searcher.results]
    tools: [fetch_page]
  writer:
    role: draft the answer from extracted claims only
    inputs: [reader.claims, goal]
    tools: []
judge:
  prompt: separate        # never the writer's own prompt
  returns: [score, diagnosed_deficiency]

body.text: Evolve the workflow by small, validated edits

body: Test-time evolution tunes a workflow from execution feedback, and it hides a trap [1]. Broad revisions can break components that already worked [1]. So in Inherit-MAS, each ordinary round starts from the latest completed candidate [1]. It may drop nodes the judge found unhelpful. Then it applies one validated edit aimed at the diagnosed weakness [1].

A subtitle system called SMART evolves just as narrowly [4]. During a test-time training phase, it translates a subset of sentences and builds series-level memory [4]. A judge-refiner loop scores candidates and turns written critiques into new agent prompts and routing policies, leaving the underlying LLMs untouched [4]. The evolved setup then translates the rest of the series [4].

Across all 15 language directions in its Subtitle Arena, SMART had the top overall MQM score [4]. MQM grades a translation by its weighted errors, so a lower penalty is better. SMART's average penalty came in 6.9% under the best competing agent system [4]. On the public MuSC benchmark, it led all four language pairs and scored 4.50 out of 5 with human raters [4]. Small edits under a strict judge compound.

body.text: Reuse a stored result only on an exact match

body: Re-running unchanged requests after every edit burns tokens for nothing [1]. Inherit-MAS adds execution inheritance, so a new candidate can reuse stored results from earlier runs [1]. The guard is strict. Reuse happens only when the full resolved request and the whole execution context match [1].

body.alt: Flow: resolve a node's request and context; on an exact match inherit the stored result, otherwise run and store.
body.caption: Execution inheritance skips a model call only when the whole request and context match.

body.text: When the new candidate executes, execution inheritance inherits eligible stored results only if the complete resolved request and execution context match, avoiding redundant model and tool calls.

body: Against the same controller with inheritance switched off, worker-token use fell 29.1% on WorkBench and 34.6% on HotpotQA [1]. Total token use fell 5.3% and 18.1% [1]. With GPT-4o-mini workers, the system completed 55.4% of WorkBench tasks and hit 49.7% joint F1 on HotpotQA FullWiki [1]. It beat EvoAgent, EvoMAS and TacoMAS, and did so again with Qwen3-32B workers [1].

Notice the gap between worker and total savings. We suspect the rest of the bill sits in parts that never get cached, such as the meta-model and the judge. We think the exact-match rule is the right default. A loose match saves more on paper. It also quietly reuses an answer to a different question.

body.text: Make every agent leave a reason behind

body: Some agent work is judged on its paper trail. Systematic literature reviews follow PRISMA, a process of screening studies and then extracting evidence from the ones kept [2]. LLM deep research tools can search and summarise, yet they leave no record of excluded studies or of where each value came from [2]. For a review, that missing trail is disqualifying.

body.alt: Bars: best screening score 0.776 macro F1 and best extraction score 0.788 F1 on expert reviews.
body.caption: The review system kept a reason for every call and still posted usable scores.

body.text: Each screening decision comes with its reason and each extracted value with its source.

body: ReviewPilot, a conversational multi-agent system, runs the PRISMA workflow from screening to extraction [2]. Researchers adjust criteria and schemas by talking to it, and a project memory keeps their settings and revisions [2]. Each screening call ships with its reason. Each extracted number points back to where it was found [2].

On epidemiological expert reviews, it outscored AgentSLR and a single-prompt LLM, with each of three underlying LLMs [2]. Its best screening result was 0.776 macro F1, and its best extraction result was 0.788 F1 [2]. F1 balances precision, the share of picks that were right, against recall, the share of right answers found. We think the trail matters more than the score. A reviewer can fix a wrong answer that cites its source.

body.text: Train the bidding along with the skills

body: Most agent teams run inside a fixed orchestration, and their members are trained apart from how the team is organised [5]. A new paper on market-based post-training, MPT, learns both at once in decentralised swarms [5]. Each agent places a bid to take part. The bids decide who acts and how the team's result becomes local training credit [5]. No central coordinator is needed [5].

The authors tested it on deep research, robot navigation and embodied crafting [5]. It beat monolithic post-training, and the agents' participation shifted as they learned [5]. With the same action policies, learned self-orchestration beat other coordination schemes [5]. Larger swarms adapted faster to related tasks and lost less when agents dropped out [5].

We find the dropout result the most practical. A team that degrades gently when one member fails is easier to run than one with a single coordinator to lose. The catch is training. Bids only turn into credit when the outcome can be scored, and plenty of business tasks have no clean score.

body.text: Give an agent a model of the one across the table

body: Agents that deal with people or other agents must reason about what the partner knows and plans, often without seeing everything [6]. Current systems lean on prompt design, memory or end-to-end shaping [6]. They rarely learn a reusable picture of the partner's state [6]. A new paper on mental models adds that picture explicitly.

Its agents carry a latent model of their counterpart [6]. From the history so far, they guess its hidden beliefs, its intentions and how it will likely react [6]. The model is a recursive Theory-of-Mind representation with first- and second-order structure [6]. In plain terms, it tracks what the partner believes and what the partner believes about you. A reward model conditioned on those beliefs scores candidate moves, and a policy learns from it [6].

Across language-only and multimodal benchmarks, the authors report better interaction quality and Theory-of-Mind scores than base agentic systems [6]. We would reach for this in negotiation or customer support, where the partner holds facts you lack. For cooperating workers that share one state, there is little hidden to infer.

body.text: Stay with one agent when the task has no seams

body: Not every task wants a team. Every extra agent adds handoffs, tokens and another place for the goal to drift [3, 1]. The steering agent helped single agents too, so supervision does not require a crowd [3]. If one model can hold the whole task and its tools in one pass, splitting it buys coordination cost and little else.

The published wins came from tasks with real seams [4, 5, 2]. Think of whole TV series that need consistent terms, review pipelines that need an audit trail, or swarms that must survive a dropout. A short, self-contained job has none of those. Give it one agent, a clear goal and a check at the end. Add a second agent when a seam appears.
What is a multi-agent system in AI?

A multi-agent system is a set of LLM-driven agents, each with its own role and tools, that split one task and pass work between them. One recent design has a meta-model write the workflow, declaring each worker's role, inputs and tool permissions [1]. A separate judge then scores each run and names what went wrong [1].
What is goal drift in AI agents?

Goal drift is when an agent or a team of agents strays from the overall goal as a long run unfolds. It wastes compute and produces unwanted results [3]. One fix adds a steering agent that watches the run [3]. A cheap check decides when to step in, and a costlier one decides how [3].
Are multi-agent systems better than a single LLM?

Sometimes, on tasks with real seams. A multi-agent review tool beat a single-prompt LLM on screening and extraction, and it left a reason for every decision [2]. A subtitle system beat rival agent systems on long series that need consistent terms [4]. On short, self-contained jobs, extra agents mostly add handoffs and tokens.
